title: The Impossible Choice of Childhood Education
author: O. Alan Noble
source: newsletter.oalannoble.com (You Are Not Your Own), October 21, 2026
summary: O. Alan Noble, linked from the Challies.com daily roundup under the title How to Choose How to Educate Your Children, addresses Christian parents crushed by the decision among public school, private Christian school, and homeschooling. Whatever they choose, some other believer will judge them, and anxiety about competition, cost, special needs, and temperament piles on. Noble argues that no schooling answer fits every family and that the choice is a matter of wisdom and Christian freedom exercised through prudence. Drawing on his book To Live Well, he lays out a sequence: survey reality, recognize the good, deliberate with prayer and wise counsel, decide without waiting for certainty, and act resolutely. He allows reassessment when new information arrives and closes by urging evangelicals to offer each other grace instead of condemnation.
points: Noble contends that no single schooling model suits every family, so the decision is a matter of wisdom and Christian freedom rather than a test of orthodoxy.
He frames the process as prudence in five steps: survey reality, identify the good, deliberate, decide, and act resolutely.

He defines the educational good as growing children in the knowledge, skills, formation, and wisdom needed to honor God and love their neighbor, which also shows what to supplement at home and church.
Parents should seek counsel but remain the ones who answer for the decision, and should not wait for certainty before choosing.
Reassessing when new information appears is part of prudence, and the community's best contribution is grace rather than condemnation.
quotes: These and a hundred other weighty questions plague Christian parents who are just trying to do their best and yet are told or feel from all sides that if they don’t get it just right they are in sin and are ruining their children forever.

To make these decisions, we must use prudence and have courage. We must prayerfully make the best decision we can with the information we have and walk it out in confidence, knowing that God honors our faithful use of prayerful reason in difficult situations.
As I see it, despite what some claim, I don’t think there is a schooling answer that fits every family. I believe that this is a matter of wisdom and Christian freedom.
Remember, ultimately you as a couple have to make this decision, but you can get some outside counsel. If you decide against what they recommend, that’s okay.
Don’t wait until you are certain that you should homeschool or attend the local public school or sign up for private school. If you wait for certainty, you’ll never decide.

If you discover that their environment isn’t healthy, that they aren’t learning, that you aren’t cut out for homeschooling, that you can’t afford private school, that your kids don’t feel safe—whatever the new information might be—then use that new information and apply prudence again.
We aren’t going to save or perfect our children by making the right education choices. Either God will care for our kids, or we’re screwed.

As evangelicals, what we can all do for each other is have more grace and support for educational decisions. They are hard to make, and we should be supporting and encouraging each other, rather than condemning and judging each other.
